entry: English politician, philanthropist and leader of the movement to abolish the [[Atlantic slave trade]]. A native of [[Kingston upon Hull]], Yorkshire, he became an independent Member of Parliament (MP) for Yorkshire (1784–1812). After an evangelical conversion in 1785, he headed the parliamentary campaign against the British slave trade for 20 years, until the Slave Trade Act 1807. His causes also included British missionary work in India, the creation of a free colony in [[Sierra Leone]] and the foundation of the Church Mission Society. His conservatism led him to support repressive legislation, which drew criticism that he ignored injustices at home. He supported the campaign for complete abolition of slavery, which led to the Slavery Abolition Act 1833. He was buried in [[Westminster Abbey]].

English Romantic poet who, with [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]], helped launch the Romantic Age in English literature through their joint publication *Lyrical Ballads* (1798). His magnum opus is generally considered to be *The Prelude*, a semi-autobiographical poem of his early years that he revised and expanded a number of times; it was titled and published posthumously by his wife. Born in Cockermouth, Cumberland, he studied at St John's College, Cambridge. In 1790 he went on a walking tour of Europe, touring the [[Alps]] extensively and visiting France, Switzerland and Italy. He is associated with the [[Lake District]], whose landscapes his works celebrate. He was Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.

German-born American film director and producer. Born in Mulhouse, Alsace-Lorraine, then part of the [[German Empire]], he emigrated to the [[United States]] in 1921, worked first for Universal Studios and by 1925 was its youngest director. He won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Director three times, for *Mrs. Miniver* (1942), *The Best Years of Our Lives* (1946) and *Ben-Hur* (1959), all of which also won Best Picture. He received 12 nominations for Best Director, more than any other director. He directed a string of classic literary adaptations, among them *Wuthering Heights* (1939), which were box-office and critical successes, and he was known as an actors' director who often propelled performers to stardom.

English Franciscan friar, scholastic philosopher and theologian. Probably born in Ockham, Surrey, he joined the Franciscan Order at an early age and studied at the [[University of Oxford]] but never became a regent master. He is widely known for [[Occam's razor]], the methodological principle that bears his name, and he wrote significant works on [[Logic]], [[Physics]] and [[Theology]]. Summoned to the papal court at Avignon in 1324 to defend his commentary on Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, he became involved in the dispute over Apostolic poverty. He later fled Avignon, sought protection under Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV in [[Munich]], and wrote treatises denouncing the pope as heretical, which led to his excommunication.

Norman king of England (r. 1066–1087) and duke of [[Normandy]] (from 1035). Illegitimate son of Duke Robert I of Normandy, he consolidated his power in Normandy by about 1060 and secured control of the county of Maine by 1062. Claiming the throne after the death of [[Edward the Confessor]] in January 1066, he invaded England and defeated Harold Godwinson at the [[Battle of Hastings]] on 14 October 1066. He suppressed subsequent English revolts in what became known as the [[Norman Conquest]]. His reign was marked by castle-building and the settlement of a new Norman nobility on English land. In 1086 he ordered the compilation of the [[Domesday Book]], a survey of English landholdings. He died while leading a campaign in northern France and was buried in Caen. His lands were divided: Normandy went to his son Robert and England to his second surviving son, William Rufus.

Dutch nobleman, Prince of Orange and leader of the Dutch revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule, which set off the [[Eighty Years' War]] (1568–1648). He is the founder of the Orange-Nassau branch and ancestor of the monarchy of the [[Netherlands]]. Initially a servant of the Habsburgs at the court of Margaret of Parma, governor of the Spanish Netherlands, he turned against Spain over the centralization of power and the persecution of Dutch [[Protestantism|Protestants]]. The most influential and politically capable of the rebels, he led the Dutch to several successes against Spain. The Spanish king declared him an outlaw in 1580, and he was assassinated in Delft. He is widely considered a heroic figure and the principal founding father of the Netherlands, and is known as *Pater Patriae* (Father of the Fatherland).

American country singer, guitarist and songwriter, a main figure of the outlaw country subgenre that developed in the early 1970s. After moving to [[Austin, Texas|Austin]] in 1972, he recorded albums such as *Shotgun Willie* (1973), *Red Headed Stranger* (1975) and *Stardust* (1978), whose success made him one of the most recognized artists in [[Country music|country music]]. He wrote country standards including "Crazy." He acted in over 30 films and is an activist for [[Biofuel|biofuels]] and the legalization of marijuana.

Skyscraper in the Loop of [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]], formerly known as the Sears Tower. Designed by Bruce Graham and Fazlur Rahman Khan of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, the 110-story, 1,451-foot (442.3 m) building opened in 1973 as the world's tallest building, a title it held for nearly 25 years. Its nine square tubes are clustered in a 3×3 matrix. It was renamed in 2009 under a naming-rights lease with the Willis Group. Its Skydeck, the highest observation deck in the United States, draws more than 1.7 million visitors a year, and [[United Airlines]] is its largest tenant.

Genus of mostly deciduous [[Tree|trees]] and [[Shrub|shrubs]] (*Salix*), also called sallows or osiers, that grows primarily on moist [[Soil|soils]] in cold and temperate regions. Narrow-leaved shrub species are called osiers and broader-leaved species sallows, from [[Old English]] *sealh*, related to the [[Latin]] word *salix*. Some arctic and alpine species are low-growing, creeping shrubs; the dwarf willow rarely exceeds 6 cm in height. Willows have soft, usually pliant, tough wood and large, fibrous roots that readily sprout from aerial parts. Most willows are dioecious, with male and female catkins on separate plants, and they are among the earliest woody plants to leaf out in spring. Its scientific name, *Salix*, was first used by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.

German politician and statesman, chancellor of [[West Germany]] from 1969 to 1974. Born Herbert Frahm in Lübeck, he fled to Norway and then Sweden during the Nazi regime and adopted the pseudonym Willy Brandt, formally taking the name in 1948. He led the [[Social Democratic Party of Germany]] from 1964 to 1987 and was the first Social Democratic chancellor since 1930. His Ostpolitik sought better relations with [[Eastern Europe]], and in 1971 he received the Nobel Peace Prize for strengthening cooperation in Western Europe. In 1970 he knelt in silence at a memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (the *Kniefall von Warschau*). He resigned in 1974 after an aide, Günter Guillaume, was exposed as an agent of the East German secret service. He was criticized from the right for his Ostpolitik and from the left for his support of American policies, including his silence on the [[Vietnam War]] until 1973.

American sprinter who overcame childhood [[Polio|polio]] to become a world-record-holding Olympic champion in [[Track and field]]. Rudolph won a bronze medal in the 4 × 100-meter relay at the 1956 Summer Olympics in [[Melbourne]], Australia. At the 1960 Summer Olympics in [[Rome]], she won three gold medals, in the 100- and 200-meter events and the 4 × 100-meter relay, becoming the first American woman to win three gold medals at a single [[Olympic Games]]. She was acclaimed as the fastest woman in the world. Her success made her an international star and a role model for Black and female athletes. She retired in 1962 as world record-holder in the 100- and 200-meter events, then became an educator and coach. She is also regarded as a civil rights and women's rights pioneer.

American professional basketball player, a center in the [[National Basketball Association]] for 14 seasons. Standing 7 feet 1 inch (2.16 m) tall, he played for the Philadelphia/San Francisco Warriors, Philadelphia 76ers and [[Los Angeles Lakers]], and won two NBA championships. He is the only player to score 100 points in a single game, and the only one to average 30 points and 20 rebounds per game in a season, which he did seven times. He holds 72 NBA records and once averaged 50 points per game in a season. Later he played [[Volleyball|volleyball]] in the short-lived International Volleyball Association.

Class of musical instruments in which a column of air inside a resonator, usually a tube, is set into vibration by the player blowing into or over a mouthpiece. Pitch depends on the length of the tube and on manual changes to its effective length, such as keys or [[Valve|valves]]. Wind instruments are grouped into [[Brass instrument|brass]] and [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] families, classified by how sound is produced rather than by material: saxophones are typically made of brass but are woodwinds. In brass instruments, such as the [[Trumpet]] and [[Tuba]], the player's lips vibrate. Woodwinds produce sound through a reed, as in the [[Clarinet]] and oboe, or by blowing across an edge, as in the [[Flute]].

Device for converting the [[Kinetic energy|kinetic energy]] of wind into electrical energy. Turbines are built in a wide range of sizes, with horizontal or vertical axes, although horizontal is most common; commercial horizontal-axis turbines usually have three blades, upwind of their towers. Vertical-axis designs include the Darrieus, the Savonius, and floating and airborne types. Blades are most commonly made of glass-fiber composites, with carbon fiber also used. Larger turbines can contribute to a domestic power supply while selling unused power back to the [[Electrical grid|electrical grid]]. Wind turbines produce among the cheapest [[Renewable energy|renewable]] energy and are clean, emitting no greenhouse gases, but their output varies with the wind rather than with demand, so they are unreliable unless energy storage is available. As of 2024, hundreds of thousands of large turbines, in wind farms, were generating over 1,136 gigawatts, with 117 GW added each year.

Capital and largest city of [[Namibia]], on a plateau about 1,700 m (5,600 ft) above sea level in the central Khomas Highland. It is the economic, political and cultural centre of the country, where most Namibian enterprises, government bodies and cultural institutions are located. The site of a hot spring known to local pastoral tribes, it was settled in 1840 by Jonker Afrikaner, captain of the Orlam, who built a stone church; later wars destroyed the settlement. Windhoek was founded a second time in 1890 by Major Curt von François, when the territory was colonized by the German Empire. After [[World War I]] it was administered by [[South Africa]] under a [[League of Nations]] mandate.

Machine powered by wind acting on vanes or sails, used chiefly to mill grain. Wind-powered machines appeared earlier: the Babylonian ruler [[Hammurabi]] had used wind power for irrigation in [[Mesopotamia]] in the 17th century BC. The first practical windmills were horizontal, or panemone, machines with six to 12 sails covered in reed matting or cloth. They first appeared in [[Iran|Persia]] in the 9th century and spread through the Middle East and Central Asia to [[China]]. Vertical windmills first appeared in northwestern Europe in the 12th century, in an area that included [[Flanders]] and northern [[France]]. The earliest certain reference in northern Europe dates from 1185, at Weedley in [[Yorkshire]]. Vertical-axle windmills were also built in small numbers in Europe during the 18th and 19th centuries as independent inventions.

Opening in a [[Wall|wall]], [[Door|door]], [[Roof|roof]] or [[Vehicle|vehicle]] that admits [[Light|light]] and sometimes allows the passage of sound and air. Modern windows are usually glazed, with a sash set in a frame, and many can be opened for ventilation or closed to exclude [[Weather|inclement weather]]. The English word derives from Old Norse *vindauga*, from *vindr* 'wind' and *auga* 'eye'. The Romans were the first known users of glass for windows, a technology likely first developed in [[Alexandria]], Egypt, around AD 100. In the 13th century BC the earliest windows were unglazed roof openings, later covered with hide, cloth or wood. Modern floor-to-ceiling windows became possible only after industrial plate glass processes were fully perfected.

Major release of the [[Windows NT]] operating system from [[Microsoft]], released on July 29, 2015. It was a free upgrade for users of [[Windows 7]], 8 and 8.1, and returned to a desktop interface with the Start menu, while introducing the Cortana assistant and Microsoft Edge, which replaced [[Internet Explorer]]. Unlike earlier NT releases, it received free feature updates on an ongoing basis. It was succeeded by [[Windows 11]] in October 2021, and it was the most popular version of Windows from January 2018 until June 2025. Support for most editions ended on October 14, 2025.

Major release of the [[Windows NT]] operating system from [[Microsoft]], released on October 5, 2021, as a successor to [[Windows 10]]. It introduced a redesigned shell with a centered Start menu and a separate Widgets panel, and it replaced [[Internet Explorer]] with the Chromium-based Microsoft Edge. Official support required [[UEFI]], Secure Boot and Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, which excluded many systems. It was the first version of Windows without a 32-bit build. In June 2025 it surpassed Windows 10 as the most installed version of Windows worldwide, and by October 2026 it held 74% of worldwide share.

Major release of the [[Windows NT]] operating system from [[Microsoft]], released to manufacturing on July 22, 2009, as the successor to Windows Vista. It fixed some of Vista's inconsistencies and added a redesigned taskbar that could pin applications and a new Action Center. Critics praised its performance and fewer User Account Control pop-ups, and it sold over 630 million copies. It was surpassed by [[Windows 10]] as the most popular version of Windows in January 2018. Extended support ended on January 14, 2020.

Family of proprietary graphical operating systems produced by [[Microsoft]] as part of its [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] product line. Windows NT 3.1 was released in 1993 for workstation and server markets, eliminating the 16-bit memory access limits of earlier Windows releases such as Windows 3.1. Windows NT was made available to consumers with [[Windows XP]] in 2001, and its technology underlies later Windows versions. It supports multiprocessing, multi-user systems, 32-bit memory addressing and portability between architectures and, in newer versions, 64-bit computing with compatibility for 32-bit software.

Major release of [[Microsoft]]'s [[Windows NT]] operating system, released to manufacturing on August 24, 2001. It was the first consumer edition of Windows not based on the Windows 95 kernel or [[MS-DOS]], succeeding Windows 2000 for business users and Windows Me for home users. Critics praised its increased performance and stability, more intuitive user interface, improved hardware support and expanded multimedia capabilities. Windows Vista succeeded it in 2007. Mainstream support ended on April 14, 2009, and extended support ended on April 8, 2014. Security updates continued until May 14, 2019.

Royal residence at Windsor, [[Berkshire]], England, about 25 miles (40 km) west of London. Built in the 11th century after the [[Norman Conquest]] by [[William the Conqueror]], it has been used by the monarch since the time of Henry I and is the longest-occupied palace in Europe. Edward III rebuilt it on a grand scale. After the [[English Civil War]], Charles II had much of the castle rebuilt with Baroque interiors. George III and George IV gave it its present state apartments. It is a popular tourist attraction and was the main residence of [[Elizabeth II]] from 2011 to 2022.

Alcoholic drink made from fermented grape juice, produced in many regions in a wide variety of styles. The earliest known traces of wine date from c. 6000 BC near [[Tbilisi]] in present-day Georgia. Its popularity spread around the Mediterranean in Classical antiquity, and it was sustained in Western Europe by monks. Monks also grew grapes and made wine for the [[Eucharist]]. In the latter half of the 19th century, the phylloxera pest largely destroyed European vineyards, which had to be replanted on American rootstock. Its alcohol content makes wine generally unhealthy to consume, although it may have cardioprotective benefits. The [[European Union]] accounts for about 45% of the world's 7.1 million hectares of vineyards.

Structure, shaped as an airfoil, that produces both [[Lift (force)|lift]] and [[Drag (physics)|drag]] while moving through air. Wing efficiency is expressed as the lift-to-drag ratio. The design and analysis of aircraft wings is a principal application of [[Aerodynamics]], a branch of [[Fluid mechanics]]. Wings with an asymmetrical cross-section are the norm in subsonic flight, while symmetrical airfoils are used in [[Aircraft|aerobatic aircraft]] because they fly the same whether upright or inverted. For a wing to produce lift, it must be at a suitable angle of attack; it deflects air downward, and the air exerts an equal and opposite force on the wing. This force arises from higher pressure beneath the wing than above it. The word wing comes from Old Norse *vængr*, and for centuries it referred mainly to the foremost limbs of [[Bird|birds]]. Equivalent foils that move through water are found on hydrofoil vessels and on [[Submarine|submarines]].
